Hypergeometric anomaly detection for co-occurring node pairs

Source: R/hypergraph_hypa.R
hypa.net_hg.Rd

The hypergraph method of hypa(). Scores pairs of nodes against a hypergeometric null that keeps every node's co-occurrence strength and otherwise pairs the nodes at random. A pair that shares far more hyperedges than the null predicts is over-represented; a pair that shares far fewer, possibly none, is under-represented. This is the undirected counterpart of hypa.default(), which applies the same null to the paths of a higher-order network, and it reports the same columns so the two read alike.

Usage

# S3 method for class 'net_hg'
hypa(x, min_count = 5L, alpha = 0.05, p_adjust = "none", top = NULL, ...)

Arguments

x

A net_hg, or a snapshot of a temporal one.

min_count

Single whole number \(\ge 1\) (default 5L). A pair is over-represented only if it co-occurs at least min_count times and under-represented only if it is expected to co-occur at least min_count times. Pairs eligible for neither are not scored.

alpha

Significance threshold for the anomaly column, a single number in (0, 0.5) (default 0.05), applied to the adjusted p-values.

p_adjust

Multiplicity correction, any stats::p.adjust method or "none" (default "none", as in LaRock et al. 2020). "BH" controls the false discovery rate within each direction.

top

Optional number of rows to keep, the most significantly over-represented first. NULL (default) keeps every scored pair.

...

Must be empty: an argument that only the sequence method takes (order, action, ...) raises hypergraphs_bad_input.

Value

A base data.frame, one row per scored pair, most significantly over-represented first (by p_adjusted_over, ties broken by ratio, then by name), with columns from, to (the pair, in the node order of the hypergraph), observed (co-occurrence count, 0 for a pair that never co-occurs), expected (the fitted \(E_{ij}\)), ratio (observed / expected), p_under, p_over, p_adjusted_under, p_adjusted_over and anomaly ("over", "under" or "normal"). The attribute "hypa_fit" records the fit of the null: converged, iterations, max_error (largest absolute strength error) and n_cooccurrences (\(m\)).

Errors of class hypergraphs_bad_input are raised for an invalid argument, and of class hypergraphs_empty_result when no pair co-occurs or no pair reaches min_count in either sense. A warning of class hypergraphs_no_converge is raised when the null cannot be fitted to tolerance.

Details

The test is analytic, so it needs no resampling. That is what makes it usable where hg_null_test() is not: hg_null_test() answers whether the hypergraph as a whole carries more repetition than chance, by Monte Carlo, and returns one row; this returns one row per pair.

Observed counts. For nodes \(i < j\), \(c_{ij}\) is the number of hyperedges that contain both (hyperedge weights are ignored; a repeated hyperedge counts each time). The total is \(m = \sum_{i<j} c_{ij}\) and the strength of node \(i\) is \(s_i = \sum_{j \ne i} c_{ij}\), so \(\sum_i s_i = 2m\).

Null model. Every unordered pair of distinct nodes with positive strength is a possible cell, whether it co-occurs or not. The expected count is \(E_{ij} = x_i x_j\), the product form of Chung and Lu (2002), with the fitness \(x\) fitted so that \(\sum_{j \ne i} E_{ij} = s_i\) for every node: the null preserves each node's observed strength, as the propensity fit of LaRock et al. (2020) preserves the in- and out-strengths of a De Bruijn graph. The fit is the damped fixed point \(x_i \leftarrow \sqrt{x_i s_i / (X - x_i)}\), \(X = \sum_k x_k\), iterated until the largest strength error falls below \(10^{-10} m\) or 10,000 sweeps have run. Each sweep costs \(O(n)\); no \(n \times n\) matrix is formed. With three or more nodes the fit has a solution with positive fitness exactly when no node takes part in every co-occurring pair. In a star-like hypergraph, where one node is in every co-occurring pair, the fit cannot converge, and the result is returned with a warning of class hypergraphs_no_converge.

Test. The propensity of a pair is \(\Xi_{ij} = m E_{ij}\), which sums to \(m^2\). The observed count \(f = c_{ij}\) is referred to a \(\mathrm{Hypergeometric}(N, K, n)\) law with \(N = m^2\), \(K = \mathrm{round}(\Xi_{ij})\) and \(n = m\) draws, whose mean is \(E_{ij}\). p_under is \(P(X \le f)\) and p_over is the strict upper tail \(P(X > f) = 1 - \) p_under, so a pair is over-represented when its HYPA score \(P(X \le f)\) exceeds \(1 - \alpha\), the rule of LaRock et al. (2020). With small counts the strict upper tail rejects more often than \(\alpha\) under the null; min_count limits the problem.

Scored pairs and classification. A pair is scored when it could be classified: when it co-occurs at least min_count times (eligible for over-representation) or is expected to co-occur at least min_count times (eligible for under-representation, including pairs that never co-occur). There are at most \(m /\) min_count pairs of the second kind, because the expected counts sum to \(m\). A scored pair is "under" when expected >= min_count and p_adjusted_under < alpha, otherwise "over" when observed >= min_count and p_adjusted_over < alpha, otherwise "normal". min_count selects the hypotheses by count, never by p-value, and the null is fitted on every pair whatever the floor, so raising the floor changes which pairs are tested but never the expected counts.

Multiple testing. LaRock et al. (2020) classify against alpha without correction, and so does the default p_adjust = "none". Any stats::p.adjust method can be applied instead. The under- and over-representation p-values are then adjusted separately, and each family is every possible pair (\(n(n-1)/2\) for the \(n\) nodes with positive strength), as in the sequence method, which adjusts over every possible path. Only the scored pairs are computed; the others enter stats::p.adjust() through its n argument, which treats them as larger p-values. Adjusting within the scored pairs alone would under-correct, because a pair enters the scored set partly through its observed count.

Time is handled by scoring a cumulative snapshot rather than by slicing into periods. Disjoint periods split a pair's evidence across cells while multiplying the number of tests, so both terms move the wrong way; a sequence of hg_snapshot(hg, at = ..., mode = "cumulative") accumulates evidence instead and shows when a pair becomes anomalous.

References

LaRock, T., Nanumyan, V., Scholtes, I., Casiraghi, G., Eliassi-Rad, T., and Schweitzer, F. (2020). HYPA: Efficient detection of path anomalies in time series data on networks. Proceedings of the 2020 SIAM International Conference on Data Mining, 460-468. doi:10.1137/1.9781611976236.52

Chung, F., and Lu, L. (2002). Connected components in random graphs with given expected degree sequences. Annals of Combinatorics, 6(2), 125-145. doi:10.1007/PL00012580

See also

hypa.default() for the same null on the paths of sequences, hg_null_test() for the Monte Carlo whole-hypergraph tests.

Examples

memberships <- data.frame(
  actor = c("a","b","c", "a","b","d", "a","b","e", "c","d","e", "a","b","f"),
  group = rep(c("g1","g2","g3","g4","g5"), each = 3)
)
hg <- group_hypergraph(memberships, node = "actor", hyperedge = "group")
hypa(hg, min_count = 2L)
#>   from to observed expected    ratio   p_under    p_over p_adjusted_under
#> 1    a  b        4 3.354836 1.192309 0.7801609 0.2198391        0.7801609
#>   p_adjusted_over anomaly
#> 1       0.2198391  normal
